splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year or whether actuaries may select assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer pension plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects revocation proceedings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, allowing the court to find violations and impose consequences even after the original term would have expired.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as specified in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating any previously presented claim — when bringing successive collateral attacks under § 2255. If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are barred from raising any claim they previously presented, in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical bar in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates can establish Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election rules such as ballot-receipt deadlines. The resolution affects whether election administration disputes are litigated before or after Election Day and has broad implications for voting procedures nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate for office has Article III standing to challenge election laws that allegedly dilute votes or change election administration rules, recognizing competitive injury as sufficient.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's speculative, pre-election concerns about ballot-counting procedures are insufficient to establish the concrete injury required for Article III standing.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards applicable to discrimination claims arising in hospitality and service industry contexts, including questions about liability and remedies. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the split, indicating the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently contested.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Adopts broader standards for establishing discrimination liability in hospitality or service establishments, with more expansive remedies available.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Applies more restrictive standards for discrimination claims in business establishments, limiting the scope of liability and available damages.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions, such as the Sentencing Guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether lenity trumps agency deference in the criminal context. Some circuits hold that lenity must prevail, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability, while others hold that agency deference trumps lenity. The issue has gained heightened significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes priority over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through interpretive rules.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (Auer/Kisor) takes priority over the rule of lenity when the Sentencing Commission interprets ambiguous Guidelines provisions, even in the criminal context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief under the First Step Act only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria or if possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. This directly controls whether district courts must sentence without regard to statutory minimums and creates disparate sentencing outcomes depending on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' as requiring all conditions.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria disqualifies a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading the provision as effectively disjunctive.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which expands 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is entitled to deference under Stinson/Kisor when the guideline text does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1's inclusion of conspiracy and other inchoate offenses in the definition of 'controlled substance offense' for career-offender purposes is a valid, authoritative interpretation of the guideline or an impermissible expansion beyond the text. The Sentencing Commission has since amended the guideline to move this language into the text, but the split remains relevant for cases sentenced under prior versions.

positions.label: Application Note 1 is entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of § 4B1.2(b) and that inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Application Note 1 exceeds the guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b)'s text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the guideline beyond its plain meaning, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the underlying substance is controlled under state law but not under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance to be federally scheduled. Some circuits hold the definition broadly encompasses any state drug offense regardless of federal scheduling, while others require a match to the federal schedules. This affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements.

positions.label: No federal-schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' broadly includes state drug offenses even if the particular substance is not controlled under federal law, finding no textual basis to graft a federal limitation.

positions.label: Federal-schedule match required
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act, applying a categorical approach.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release, either alone or in combination with other factors. This split has been deepened by the Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to § 1B1.13(b)(6), which some circuits have held exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A), and that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement to the contrary exceeds its authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release at revocation proceedings, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the purpose of a sentence imposed upon revocation of supervised release may include punishment for the violating conduct. The Sixth Circuit's precedent in United States v. Lewis allows district courts to expressly punish defendants at revocation, placing it at the extreme of the circuit split, while other circuits require revocation sentences to focus on the breach of trust rather than additional punishment.

positions.label: Punishment for violations is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may impose revocation sentences that expressly punish defendants for conduct violating their supervised release conditions.

positions.label: Revocation sentence should address breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the defendant's breach of the court's trust inherent in the supervised release violation, not as additional punishment for the underlying violating conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions about the terms of custody (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring civil rights claims under Bivens or other statutes.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges that affect the execution of a sentence but do not directly challenge its fact or duration, such as BOP decisions on prerelease custody transfers. The Supreme Court noted but did not resolve this question in Preiser v. Rodriguez, and circuits have reached irreconcilable conclusions.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for execution-of-sentence challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions about the execution of a sentence, including prerelease custody determinations, must be brought as habeas corpus petitions rather than civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions available for conditions challenges
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions or terms of confinement that do not seek immediate or speedier release may be brought as civil rights claims and are not limited to habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal appeal deadline applies to an order on a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is the 30-day civil deadline or the 14-day criminal deadline. The majority view treats the motion as a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, while a minority applies the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the shorter 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between filing a Chapter 13 petition and converting to Chapter 7 belongs to the bankruptcy estate or the debtors. The Ninth Circuit holds it belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtors, interpreting § 348(f)(1)(A) to protect good-faith converting debtors from losing post-petition appreciation.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in property equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtors
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by excluding post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation from the bankruptcy estate, consistent with the statute's structure and legislative history.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal court filings containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit has held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is an immediately appealable collateral order because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' effectively unreviewable after final judgment, while other circuits have questioned whether such orders satisfy the collateral order doctrine's strict requirements.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal medical information are immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal does not satisfy the collateral order doctrine because the right can be adequately vindicated through other means, including post-judgment appeal.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits have divided on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically exclude transgender women from women's sports teams, with some recognizing viable as-applied equal protection challenges where individuals have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and others upholding categorical exclusions.

positions.label: Categorical bans may violate Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women's participation in women's sports may violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Categorical bans survive Equal Protection scrutiny
positions.summary: Holds that state laws categorically restricting sports participation based on biological sex survive intermediate scrutiny and do not violate the Equal Protection Clause.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
